subtitle: Practice being answerable in daily work: know who you answer to, make it easy to be told you are wrong, own a mistake and its effect without defending it, and follow through, including handing formal matters to the right partner.
audience: For anyone who leads or wants to, with or without a title, and for supervisors in their first year who are learning what it means to answer for decisions that reach other people's work and lives.

lessons.title: Who you answer to in public service
objectives: Explain accountability in public service as answerability to the people served, colleagues, the public and the law, rather than blame.
Identify the people a decision in your own work reaches and whose view of it is missing.
Distinguish a duty set by law or policy from good practice you choose.
Draft a short answerability map for one piece of work you lead or support.
lessons.teaching:
Accountability in public service means being answerable, not being blamed. When you hold a public role, your work reaches people who did not choose you and often cannot go elsewhere. People receiving services, family members, partners and coworkers may need an explanation of decisions that affect them. Give relevant information through an appropriate channel while protecting private records and respecting each person’s authority to receive it. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide, written for state employees, describes state leaders as accountable to all Minnesotans and expects leaders to take accountability for their own actions. Blame looks back for someone to punish. Answerability looks at what happened, who it affected and what happens next.

Public service involves responsibilities to people receiving services, colleagues who depend on your work, and the public that funds it. Law and agency policy define some of these responsibilities, while the practices suggested here help you explain decisions and respond to concerns. Minnesota's code of ethics for executive branch employees, section 43A.38 of Minnesota Statutes, says that when an employee believes a conflict of interest may exist, it is the employee's duty to avoid the situation. Other habits in this course, such as asking for correction or reporting back, are good practice you choose. Keep the two apart.

A short map shows who a decision reaches. First, name the decision or piece of work. Second, list who it reaches: the people served, partners, coworkers, the public and any rule that applies. Third, ask whose experience you have not heard and how you would find out. Fourth, ask who decides each part and what evidence you have. Many of us learned at work that being accountable means answering to the person above us. That is a real duty. But a habit that only checks upward can miss the people a decision lands on, often the people with the least say in it.

Being answerable does not mean you decide everything or carry every outcome alone. You can explain your own choices, invite questions and fix what is yours to fix. Formal conduct, discipline and complaint matters follow authorized agency processes, with responsibilities shared among management, Human Resources, labor relations and Equal Opportunity and Access as applicable. Under section 43A.38, a possible conflict of interest is yours to avoid and can be determined by you, your appointing authority or the commissioner, so raise it promptly. Answerability is the daily practice underneath those processes. It is not a substitute for them.
lessons.keyPoint: Accountability means being answerable to the people served, colleagues, the public and the law. It asks what happened, for whom and what comes next. It does not start by asking whom to blame.
lessons.example: Practice case: Desmond, a program consultant in disability services, has drafted guidance for lead agencies on a waiver service change. His manager, Henrietta wants it sent Friday. Ruthanne, a lead agency partner, says one section will confuse families. Wren, a self-advocate who co-chairs the division's advisory group, notes the plain-language summary was never tried with anyone who uses the service. Desmond finds both concerns fair, though the policy itself is correct.
lessons.question: What should Desmond do?
choices: Send the guidance Friday as his manager asked, and keep Ruthanne's and Wren's points on file so they shape the next revision of the guidance.
Tell Henrietta what he found, propose a short dated delay for the two weak parts, and tell Ruthanne and Wren what will change and when.
Hold the guidance until every lead agency partner and advisory member agrees with the wording, so that nobody can later say they were not heard.
feedback: Meeting the deadline matters, and the policy is correct. But families would receive guidance with an identified risk of confusion, and the people who flagged it never hear what he did.
This is the strongest response. Desmond answers upward and outward: his manager decides with the facts, the delay is limited and dated, and the people who raised concerns hear back.
Wanting everyone heard is a good instinct. But open-ended agreement leaves lead agencies and families without guidance, and it hands the decision to whoever objects last.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider who comes to mind first when you think about whom you answer to. Which people does your work reach who rarely come to mind at all?
lessons.action: Pick one piece of work you lead or support. Write a short map of who it reaches, who decides each part and one group whose view you have not heard. Note one way to hear from them before your next decision.

check.question: Which statement best describes accountability as this lesson uses it?
check.correct: Explaining your choices and their effects to the people served, colleagues, the public and the law.
wrong: Making sure someone is identified and corrected each time a decision goes wrong for a person served.
Answering mainly to your supervisor, who then explains your work to the other people it reaches.
check.feedback: Answerability includes explaining relevant decisions, their effects and next steps through appropriate channels. Protect private information and follow the authorized process. Answering only upward can overlook people affected by the decision; identifying a responsible person is useful when it supports action rather than blame.

lessons.title: Making it easy to be told you are wrong
objectives: Describe how differences in power and role change what people are willing to say to a leader.
Plan at least two ways to invite correction that do not depend on people speaking up first in a group.
Compare how inviting correction looks as a habit at different points on the Intercultural Development Continuum.
Explain why acting on correction, and saying so, matters as much as asking for it.
lessons.teaching:
An open door is not the same as an easy door. Telling a leader they are wrong carries risk, and the risk is larger for people with less power: a newer employee, someone in a temporary role, a provider whose license you review or a person whose services depend on your decision. A perspective published by the federal Patient Safety Network describes team psychological safety as a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, and names hierarchy and authoritarian leadership among the barriers. Silence alone does not establish either the quality of the work or why someone has not raised a concern.

Leaders can lower the cost of speaking up, though the evidence has limits. In Deloitte research on inclusive leadership, Bernadette Dillon and Juliet Bourke describe humility as admitting mistakes, acknowledging limits and seeking others' input. A 2026 umbrella review by Gonzalez and colleagues found listening, transparency and sharing power among the leader behaviors linked to psychological safety, and the authors suggest that leaders model vulnerability, for example by admitting mistakes. Most of this research comes from health care and general management studies, not public human services. The reviewers note that the usual definition reflects a Western, individualist view and that culture, race and ethnicity are little examined. Consider how your response to disagreement may affect someone’s willingness to raise a later concern.

The following program examples use vocabulary from IDI, LLC’s Intercultural Development Continuum to compare approaches to correction. They are illustrations, not a way to determine anyone’s orientation. A Minimization habit sounds fair: my door is open to everyone, so anyone can tell me. An Acceptance habit notices that people learned different rules about whether and how to disagree with someone above them, and that your own rule is only one of them. An Adaptation habit changes the method. You ask a specific question, such as which step in this checklist does not work. You offer a written route and a later one-to-one. You go first by naming something you may have missed, and report what you changed. These describe habits, not people. Nobody should guess or label a colleague's orientation.

Asking for correction is the easier half of the work. Explain what you changed after hearing feedback and, when you leave something unchanged, give the reason. Do not pressure someone to identify coworkers merely to establish who disagrees with you. An authorized complaint process may need relevant facts, so explain any reporting duties and confidentiality limits. Route possible harassment, discrimination or accommodation concerns through the applicable agency process rather than treating them only as suggestions.
lessons.keyPoint: If nobody tells you that you are wrong, check the cost of speaking before you trust the silence. Make correction easy for people with less power, act on it and say what you changed.
lessons.example: Practice case: Yusra has supervised an eligibility team for five months. She often tells the team her door is always open, and nobody has raised a concern. Since she introduced a new intake checklist, returned applications have gone up. In passing, Ofelia, who joined on a temporary appointment, says that some people think the checklist skips a step, then quickly adds that it is probably fine. Yusra wrote the checklist herself, and her manager praised it.
lessons.question: What should Yusra do next?
choices: Ask Ofelia privately who thinks the checklist skips a step and exactly what they said, so she can follow up with each person directly.
Remind the team at the next meeting that her door is always open and that anyone with a concern about the checklist should come and see her.
Tell the team she may have the checklist wrong, ask which step fails, offer written and one-to-one routes, and report what she changes.
feedback: Yusra wants specifics, which is right. But asking Ofelia to name coworkers puts the newest, least secure person in the middle and may discourage another comment.
The invitation is sincere, but it repeats the method that already produced silence. People who see risk in speaking still have to come forward alone and in person.
This is the strongest response. Yusra goes first, asks a specific question, offers more than one way to answer and closes the loop, so people have more than one opportunity to raise a concern.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall a time you told someone above you they were wrong, or chose not to. What made it feel safe or unsafe, and what might people risk by correcting you?
lessons.action: Choose one decision or document you own. This week, ask two people with less say than you one specific question about what does not work, offer a way to answer in writing, and tell them what you changed.

check.question: A leader says, "My door is always open, so anyone can tell me if I am wrong." What does this habit miss?
check.correct: That speaking up costs more for people with less power, so one open invitation is not equally usable.
wrong: That people speak up most honestly when the leader asks them directly, in front of the whole group.
That people with a real concern will usually raise it in a team meeting, where it can be discussed openly.
check.feedback: An open invitation treats everyone's position as the same. People with less power carry more risk in disagreeing, so leaders ask specific questions, offer more than one route and show what changed.

lessons.title: Owning a mistake without defending it
objectives: Describe a mistake by what happened and its effect on another person, without explaining it away.
Distinguish an explanation that helps repair from one that defends you.
Plan a repair that addresses the effect on the person and changes the practice that allowed the mistake.
Identify which parts of a repair you can offer and which belong to a supervisor or a formal process.
lessons.teaching:
Owning a mistake starts with what happened to the other person, not with your reasons. When public servants get something wrong, the effect often lands on someone with little power to push back: a family that missed a deadline, a provider that changed staffing or a coworker who redid work. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide lists admitting that you are not always right among the expert behaviors for leading yourself. It is a skill you can practice, and a plain structure makes it easier.

A clear ownership statement names what you did, its effect on the other person and what you are doing now. In plain words: I sent the letter with the wrong due date. Say the effect as the other person experienced it, and ask about what you do not know: you moved staff and changed people's schedules to meet a date that was not real, so what else did it cost you? Then say what you are doing now and when. Keep your reasons short and put them after the effect. An explanation that helps the person know what to expect is useful. An explanation that shifts the weight onto the template, the system or the workload is defending, even when it is true.

Repair puts right the effect on the person, changes the step that let the mistake through and reports back. First, put right what you can for the person who was affected, and check with them whether it actually helps. Second, examine the step that let the mistake through and make an authorized change that reduces the chance of recurrence. Check whether the change works. Third, tell the people who were affected what you changed. Many of us learned to fix errors quietly and move on, because it feels less awkward. A correction without an explanation may leave the affected person without information about what changed or how to raise a remaining concern.

Part of owning a mistake is knowing which parts of the repair are yours. You can acknowledge the mistake, correct your own work and change your own practice. You should not promise outcomes you do not control, such as waiving a requirement, changing a licensing decision or offering compensation. Those belong to your supervisor and the responsible program area, and legal questions belong to legal counsel. If the mistake may have exposed private data, follow the agency’s incident-reporting process promptly. Possible discrimination or harassment also requires the designated complaint route. Explain the facts and immediate support needs without conducting an independent investigation or waiting to prove a violation.
lessons.keyPoint: Name what you did and what it cost the other person before you give any reasons. Then repair two things, the effect on that person and the step that let the mistake through, and tell them what changed.
lessons.example: Practice case: Corwin, a licensing reviewer in disability services, sent a day services provider a letter asking for a response to a review finding. The letter gave a due date two weeks too early. Imelda, who runs the small provider, moved staff and rescheduled several people's activities to meet it. She calls, upset. Corwin sees that he copied the date from an earlier letter. His supervisor, Thandiwe, is out until Monday, and Imelda asks whether the finding itself still stands.
lessons.question: What should Corwin say and do?
choices: Tell Imelda plainly he gave the wrong date and ask what it cost, send the correct date today, check the finding with Thandiwe Monday, and fix the copy step.
Send a corrected letter today with a short note asking the provider to disregard the earlier date, and leave any conversation about the error for Thandiwe on Monday.
Apologize that the letter template caused confusion, explain that the date carried over from an earlier letter, and reassure Imelda the finding will likely be dropped.
feedback: This is the strongest response. Corwin names his own error and its effect, repairs what he can today, takes the finding to the right person and closes the gap that caused it.
The record gets fixed quickly, which helps. But Imelda hears nothing about what went wrong or what it cost her program, and the copy step that caused it stays in place.
The facts about the template may be true, but leading with them shifts the weight off Corwin. Saying the finding will likely be dropped promises a decision that is not his to make.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall a mistake of yours that affected someone else. What did you say first, and what did the other person most need to hear first?
lessons.action: Think of a recent small error in your own work, even one already fixed. Write the three-part ownership statement: what you did, its effect on someone else and what you are doing now. Then change one step so it is less likely to recur.

check.question: Which response owns a mistake rather than defending it?
check.correct: "I gave you the wrong date, and you changed staffing to meet it. What else did it cost you? The correct date comes today."
wrong: "I'm sorry for the confusion. The date carried over from an earlier letter, and a corrected letter goes out today."
"I'm sorry this happened. We are short-staffed right now, but I have asked everyone to double-check dates from now on."
check.feedback: Ownership names what you did and its effect on the other person, asks what you do not know and says what happens next. The other two lead with reasons and never name what the error cost Imelda's program.

lessons.title: Following through and knowing what belongs elsewhere
objectives: Plan how to keep a commitment visible and close the loop with the people it affects, including when the answer is no or not yet.
Identify matters that belong to Human Resources, labor relations or the equal opportunity office rather than to an informal fix.
Explain how handing a matter to a formal process differs from dropping it.
Draft a short, dated update on one open commitment.
lessons.teaching:
People need usable information about a commitment to plan their next steps and raise unresolved concerns. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide connects building trust with following through on commitments and communicating openly. A commitment can be missed when its next step, responsible person or deadline is unclear. Without an update, the people waiting may not know whether the work is delayed, finished or no longer planned.

Closing the loop means telling people where a commitment stands, even when the news is not good. A useful update says what you said you would do, what you have done, what is still open, what you decided not to do and why, and when you will next report. If the answer is no, say so and give the reason. People can plan around a clear no far better than around silence, and a clear no is still a way of answering to them. For shared work, keep an appropriate status list that identifies the commitment and next update. Keep personnel, medical and complaint details in their authorized records and channels rather than a shared team list. Explain only what the recipients are authorized to receive.

Some matters that surface while you follow through belong to a formal process. A possible accommodation request goes to Human Resources, a concern about harassment, discrimination or retaliation goes to Human Resources and the equal opportunity office, and a labor agreement question goes to labor relations. When a commitment turns into a formal matter, your promise changes shape. You can no longer promise the result, but you can still promise to move it today, to tell people where it went and to report on the parts that stay yours. Talk with the person privately, not in front of the team. Promising a result or settling it yourself can skip protections that exist for that person.

Handing a matter on is not the same as dropping it. You stay answerable for the parts that remain yours: telling people where the matter went, in general terms that protect privacy, keeping the rest of the commitment moving and checking back when you said you would. For any commitment, ask the closing question: what happened, for whom, and what will I keep, change or stop? Then give that answer to the people who were waiting.
lessons.keyPoint: Give dated updates on commitments, including a clear no or not yet. Refer formal matters through the authorized process and continue the work within your role. An update does not by itself mean the underlying work is complete.
lessons.example: Practice case: At a team meeting two months ago, Augustin, who manages a contracts team, promised to review how after-hours coverage is assigned and report back within a month. He has not. When he raises it again, Pilar says the coverage schedule has twice kept her from medical appointments and that she asked Augustin for a change weeks ago. Lorcan says he thinks the rotation ignores the overtime rules in the labor agreement. Others ask when anything will actually change.
lessons.question: What should Augustin do next?
choices: Fix it on the spot: move Pilar off evening coverage starting next week and announce a new rotation that he believes follows the overtime rules.
Own the delay, see Pilar privately so her request reaches Human Resources, send the overtime question to labor relations, and set a dated update.
Explain that both issues now sit with Human Resources and labor relations, so the coverage review is out of his hands and closes until they decide.
feedback: Acting quickly answers the frustration in the room. But it settles Pilar's request in public and outside the accommodation process, and a rotation based on his reading of the contract may not hold.
This is the strongest response. Augustin owns the missed date, keeps Pilar's request private and routed, gets the contract question to the right partner and keeps the rest moving.
Routing is right, but closing the whole review drops the parts that remain his. The team hears another promise fade, and the people waiting have no date for an answer.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a promise you made at work that faded. What did the people waiting hear from your silence, and what would a short update have told them?
lessons.action: Pick one commitment you made in the past month. This week, send a short update on what you did, what is still open and when you will next report. If part belongs to Human Resources, labor relations or the equal opportunity office, make the referral and share an appropriate status update without disclosing private details.

check.question: A matter you committed to fix turns out to belong to labor relations. What does staying accountable mean now?
check.correct: Hand it to labor relations promptly, say in general terms where it went and keep the rest moving.
wrong: Settle the matter yourself first so the team is not kept waiting, then let labor relations know what you decided.
Hand it to labor relations and treat the commitment as closed, since it is no longer yours to answer for.
check.feedback: Formal matters go to the responsible partner, and you stay answerable for the rest: where it went, what remains yours and when people will hear next. Settling it first skips protections, and closing it drops the people who were waiting.

cards.back: Being able and willing to explain what you did, its effect and what comes next to the people your work reaches. It looks forward, where blame looks for someone to punish.
As a Patient Safety Network perspective describes it, a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, such as admitting an error or disagreeing with a leader.
A plain account of a mistake: what you did, its effect on the other person and what you are doing now, with any reasons kept short and placed last.
Action that puts right what you can for the person affected and changes the step that let the mistake through, followed by telling them what changed.
Telling the people affected where a commitment stands, including no or not yet, what was decided and why, and when they will hear from you next.

aid.heading: Before a decision that affects others
items: List who the decision reaches: people served, partners, coworkers, the public and any rule that applies.
Name one group whose view you have not heard and how you will hear it.
Note who decides each part and what evidence you have.
Ask someone with less say than you one specific question about what might not work.

aid.heading: When you get something wrong
items: Say what you did and its effect before giving any reason.
Ask what the mistake cost that you do not yet know.
Repair what you can now, and do not promise decisions that belong to others.
Change the step that let the mistake through and tell people what changed.
Follow the applicable incident or complaint reporting process promptly if private data, discrimination or harassment may be involved.

aid.heading: When you follow through
items: Keep a shared list of work commitments and status updates; protect personnel, medical and complaint details in their authorized channels.
Give a dated update, including no and not yet.
Talk privately about a possible accommodation request and route it to Human Resources.
Send harassment, discrimination and retaliation concerns to Human Resources and the equal opportunity office.
Take labor agreement questions to labor relations, and keep the rest of the commitment moving.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Competency Definition Guide: Developing Leader Competencies for State of Minnesota Employees (March 2024)
sources.note: Supports that state leaders are described as accountable to all Minnesotans, take accountability for their own actions, admit they are not always right and build trust through follow-through. An expectations guide, not policy.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes — Section 43A.38, Code of Ethics for Employees in the Executive Branch (2026)
sources.note: Supports that an employee who believes a conflict of interest may exist must avoid it, and that a conflict can be determined by the employee, the appointing authority or the commissioner. Read in part; not legal advice.

sources.title: Dillon, B. and Bourke, J. — The Six Signature Traits of Inclusive Leadership: Thriving in a Diverse New World, Deloitte University Press (2016)
sources.note: Supports the description of humility as admitting mistakes, acknowledging limits and seeking others' input. Consulting research from 2016, based on 17 interviews in six countries and a literature review, not peer reviewed; described in our own words.

sources.title: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, Patient Safety Network — Annual Perspective: Psychological Safety of Healthcare Staff (2022)
sources.note: Supports the definition of team psychological safety and hierarchy and authoritarian leadership as barriers to it. Health care setting; a contractor-written perspective, so read as one summary of the research.

sources.title: Gonzalez et al. — An Umbrella Review of Relational Enablers of Psychological Safety and Identity-Related Gaps in the Evidence: Implications for Healthcare and Organizational Settings (2026)
sources.note: Supports listening, transparency and sharing power as leader enablers, the authors' suggestion to model vulnerability, and limits: a Western, individualist definition and little study of race and ethnicity. Mostly health care.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDC)
sources.note: Supports the continuum's orientations, including Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation, used here only as shared vocabulary for habits. The course does not assess, place or label anyone on the continuum.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation Policy
sources.note: Supports employee complaint reporting and supervisors’ additional referral responsibilities. The public copy uses an earlier division name; confirm current contacts and procedures through the DHS intranet.
